jsx-no-undef__invalid__00.reason: Upstream's own scope walk decides a plain JSX tag is undefined; this checker asks TypeScript, and a span with no entity is missing evidence rather than proof that no binding exists. Upstream reports the return once, whichever way the chain nests.

The checker names the derivation that will not update, and there are two of them, so `d` and `e` each get an SC1006. Upstream anchors its one report on the reactive read at the bottom of the chain.

reactivity__invalid__23.reason: Upstream's single `expectedFunctionGotExpression` report covers a component prop read installed directly as an event listener; the checker preserves both semantic consequences. Both rules map to upstream's one `reactivity` rule, so both count against its expected 1.

reactivity__invalid__30.reason: Upstream's single `noAsyncTrackedScope` covers both halves of an async effect; the checker splits them. SC5004 (v1/no-async-tracked-scope) reports the scope -- this createEffect callback is async, so tracking stops at the first await -- and SC1002 (v1/reactive-read-after-await) reports the specific read of `count` that lands after it. Both rules are in the set upstream's one `reactivity` rule maps onto, so both count against its expected 1.

imports__invalid__00.reason: Upstream's imports fix relocates the specifier: it deletes the name from the wrong declaration and splices it into a declaration of the right module. The checker's fix rewrites the offending module specifier string in place instead, so no name moves between statements. Both end with a program importing the same bindings from the same modules. Here the wrong declaration is the whole file, and upstream's replacement statement ends with a newline, so its recorded output carries a trailing "\n" that an in-place specifier rewrite has no reason to add.

imports__invalid__05.reason: Upstream's imports fix relocates the specifier: it deletes the name from the wrong declaration and splices it into a declaration of the right module. The checker's fix rewrites the offending module specifier string in place instead, so no name moves between statements. Both end with a program importing the same bindings from the same modules. Both declarations are wrong in this case -- `createEffect` from "solid-js/web" and `render` from "solid-js" -- and the checker corrects both in one pass. Upstream's output is an intermediate state a second lint pass would carry further; ours is the finished program.
